note: Original operational definitions adapted for actionable triage, not a verbatim or exhaustive reproduction of the normative glossary. Read official glossary for precise legal/technical wording.

terms.operational_meaning: Requirements that determine whether the specified level can be claimed; primary authority is the WCAG 2.1 recommendation.
Implementation guidance, notes and examples explain requirements but do not create additional obligations.
A relied-on technique must interoperate with users’ assistive technology and accessible browser or user-agent support; generic syntax support is not enough.
Significant change to viewport, user agent, focus or content meaning that may disorient without awareness; changing a panel’s content is not automatically context change.
An alternative that fully conforms at the target level, gives equivalent information/function in same language, stays current, and satisfies accessible reachability constraints.
A series of actions needed to complete an activity; all pages in such a sequence matter for conformance.
The assessed web page includes resources and UI states rendered together, not merely one isolated component.
Unsupported or otherwise nonconforming content must not prevent the rest of the page being used; four specified SCs apply to all page content.
W3C threshold is at least 18pt normal or 14pt bold for applicable Latin-script text; consider equivalent sizes for CJK; use rendered author-defined sizing.
Relationship between relative luminance of two colors; compare actual required foreground and background pairs under usual presentation.
Equivalent text serving the same purpose as non-text content; quality and semantics depend on context.
Narration of significant visual information not already available in primary soundtrack, often inserted in existing dialogue gaps.
Synchronized accessible information covering speech and other meaningful sound cues, unlike dialogue-only subtitles.
Sequenced textual representation of audiovisual information and interactive outcomes; more than a brief summary.
Accessible name is the string exposed to software; visible label is what users perceive; 2.5.3 requires visible words appear within the accessible name.
User-entered information rejected because missing required content or invalid format/value; explicit text identification applies when automatically detected.
An update about action result, wait state, progress or error that does not itself constitute a change of context.
An exception normally requires that removing the feature fundamentally changes information/function, not that it is aesthetically preferred.
A single contact point such as one mouse pointer, finger or stylus interaction; path or multi-finger alternatives are separate requirements.
Standardized CSS visual unit; accessibility zoom/reflow and target size are measured in CSS pixels, not device pixel count.
Information or relationships that user agents and assistive technology can extract from supported markup/accessibility semantics.
Reused navigation components maintain their relative order across pages unless user initiates a change.
Data intended to be accessed by users (such as account records), relevant to error prevention safeguards.
One documented path that W3C believes can satisfy a specific SC in suitable conditions; the specific technique is not mandatory.
A known pattern that fails an SC under documented conditions; check applicability and qualifying alternate content.
